sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
August 2026 delivered a broadly constructive month for global equities, with the S&P 500 advancing **+2.7%** to **7,686**, the Nasdaq Composite gaining **+3.9%** to **26,371**, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average adding **+1%** to **53,186** — marking the Dow's fifth consecutive positive month. Developed-market leadership was anchored in North America and continental Europe, with Germany's DAX striking a fresh all-time high of **26,570** and Japan's Nikkei 225 sustaining a formidable year-to-date gain of approximately **+30%**.

The primary driver was a blowout Q2 2026 earnings season, particularly within the technology sector, where AI-exposed names demonstrated that the cycle is maturing from infrastructure buildout into tangible monetisation. Energy (**+7.0%**), Information Technology (**+6.3%**), Materials (**+6.0%**), and Health Care (**+4.9%**) led US sector returns, reflecting the simultaneous tailwinds of AI earnings momentum and surging crude prices driven by Middle East supply disruption.

A dramatic final session on August 31 introduced volatility: US military strikes against Iranian positions sent the Dow tumbling **374 points** intraday and drove crude sharply higher, generating broad profit-taking ahead of September. Despite the end-of-month shock, the overall monthly tape remained positive across virtually all developed markets, a testament to the resilience of corporate earnings fundamentals in the current cycle.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes: AI Mega-Earnings Supercycle Revalidates the Thesis -- The singular force animating global equity markets in August was a Q2 2026 earnings season of historic proportions, which emphatically revalidated the AI investment thesis with reported financials rather than narrative alone. Blended year-over-year S&P 500 EPS growth clocked in at **+50.4%** — the highest quarterly growth rate in recent memory — with the technology sector surging **+74%** in profits as mega-caps including Alphabet, Amazon, and Nvidia monetised AI infrastructure investments at scale. Of the 88% of S&P 500 companies that had reported by early August, 86% beat consensus estimates, and full-year CY2026 EPS growth projections were revised upward to approximately **+30%**. Critically, market leadership broadened: enterprise software outperformed semiconductors for a second consecutive month, signalling a healthy transition from pure infrastructure spending toward application-layer monetisation, and expanding the earnings base supporting elevated equity multiples.

Iran War and Strait of Hormuz Crisis Reprices Energy Risk -- The US-Iran conflict remained the dominant geopolitical overhang of August, with Middle East tensions escalating materially through the month and culminating in fresh US military strikes on August 30 that rattled risk markets in the final session. Brent crude surged **+8.39%** to settle at **$90.80/bbl**, touching an intra-month high near **$95/bbl** as Strait of Hormuz vessel crossings fell sharply on the day of the strikes; Kpler data showed throughput at the chokepoint halved on August 30 alone. WTI crude finished near **$87/bbl**, pushing US energy sector returns to **+7.0%** for the month and reigniting inflationary fears that complicate the rate-cutting cycle narrative. The geopolitical risk premium embedded in energy prices is now a structural feature of the 2026 macro landscape, cascading into petrochemicals, shipping rates, and the inflation arithmetic faced by energy-import-dependent economies across Europe and APAC.

Jackson Hole Hawkish Shock -- Warsh Signals Rates May Rise Again -- Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh delivered his first Jackson Hole keynote address on August 28 with a decisively hawkish message that blindsided rate markets. Warning that the Fed "may still have work to do" on inflation and declining to signal any easing timeline, Warsh's remarks triggered an immediate repricing of the rate path: September rate-hike probabilities surged from **36%** to **67%** in a single session, the 2-year Treasury yield spiked to **4.34%**, and the 30-year UST briefly touched **5.34%** — its highest since summer 2007. The dollar index firmed, equity markets surrendered intraday gains on the day of the speech, and bond markets entered September on edge. The episode underscored a regime shift in Fed communication under Warsh: investors who entered 2026 positioned for a cutting cycle have been forced to dramatically revise their frameworks as energy-driven inflation and a robust labour market validate a more restrictive stance.

Bank of Japan Normalisation Reshapes APAC and Carry Trade Dynamics -- The Bank of Japan's accelerating policy normalisation was the defining macro theme for APAC markets and a major cross-asset force globally, with the central bank's policy summary explicitly flagging upside inflation risks and a faster-than-expected rate-hike trajectory. Markets priced near-certain probability of a **25bp** hike at the September BOJ meeting — subsequently delivered, taking the policy rate to **1.25%**, its highest since 1995. USD/JPY oscillated near **157** as the yen faced persistent carry-trade selling despite the hawkish BOJ signalling, the US-Japan rate differential remaining overwhelmingly in favour of dollar-funded carry. The Nikkei 225 traded in the **66,400–68,700** range throughout August, paradoxically supported by yen weakness lifting repatriated corporate earnings, even as rising JGB yields created friction for domestic bond portfolios. The BOJ normalisation story is the most consequential structural variable for APAC portfolio managers, with global carry-trade unwind risk a persistent tail scenario.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets delivered a standout August, with the S&P 500 gaining **+2.7%** to close at **7,686.14** and the Nasdaq Composite advancing **+3.9%** to **26,370.89**. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added **+1%** to **53,185.90**, securing its fifth consecutive monthly advance despite surrendering **374 points** in the final session of the month following US military strikes on Iran. The month's performance was underwritten by a Q2 earnings season in which 86% of reporting S&P 500 companies beat consensus, with blended year-over-year EPS growth of **+50.4%** led by a **+74%** surge in technology sector profits.

AI monetisation moved from thesis to demonstrated financial reality in August. Alphabet and Amazon recognised material mark-to-market gains on AI equity holdings, while Nvidia issued strong forward guidance on August 26 that reinvigorated the semiconductor supply chain. Critically, enterprise software outperformed chips for a second straight month, reflecting the AI cycle's graduation from infrastructure buildout to application-layer adoption. This broadening of earnings drivers is constructive for index sustainability, reducing concentration risk in single-name or sub-sector narratives.

Federal Reserve Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole address on August 28 introduced the most significant policy uncertainty of the month, pushing September rate-hike odds to **67%** and pressuring rate-sensitive equities in the final days of trading. A tame July CPI print in mid-August had provided an earlier tailwind to rate-cut optimism; the Warsh speech partially reversed that narrative, leaving markets with a more complex forward rate path. Full-year CY2026 EPS growth estimates of **+30%** remain the fundamental anchor supporting valuations.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities posted mixed but broadly positive returns in August. Germany's DAX was the regional standout, closing at a fresh all-time high of **26,569.99** on August 28, driven by a resilient industrial earnings cycle and improving export demand. The FTSE 100 traded in the region of **10,800** (approx., verify before merging), buoyed by its heavy energy and mining sector weighting as Brent crude gained **+8.39%** for the month. The CAC 40 underperformed continental peers, weighed by consumer discretionary weakness and politically driven risk premia.

The ECB held no scheduled meeting in August, but the lingering effect of its June **25bp** rate hike — lifting the deposit facility rate to **2.25%** — continued to exert upward pressure on eurozone sovereign yields. Italian BTP spreads versus German Bunds widened modestly as markets repriced ECB easing timelines further out in response to oil-driven headline inflation re-acceleration, elevating risk premia on higher-debt eurozone sovereigns.

Europe's macro outlook sits at an uncomfortable intersection: energy-intensive industries face a stagflationary squeeze from the Hormuz-driven oil price surge, while the ECB must weigh external commodity inflation against softening domestic demand. The DAX's outperformance reflects Germany's export-sector resilience and structural cost competitiveness at current EUR levels, but the broader eurozone growth trajectory faces meaningful headwinds from elevated energy costs and tighter monetary conditions heading into Q4.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japan's Nikkei 225 was the regional leader in August, trading in the **66,400–68,700** range as a persistently weak yen — with USD/JPY near **157** — provided an ongoing structural tailwind for export-oriented corporates through higher yen-denominated repatriated earnings. The Bank of Japan's accelerating normalisation narrative paradoxically supported equities, as markets interpreted explicit hawkish signalling as confirmation of genuine wage and economic growth rather than destabilising tightening. Japan's year-to-date equity advance of approximately **+30%** as of late August made the Nikkei the strongest-performing major developed-market index globally.

Chinese equities diverged by exchange. The Shanghai Composite edged modestly positive on the back of targeted domestic stimulus measures and stabilising manufacturing activity, though the index remained negative year-to-date at approximately **-2.2%** — a reflection of persistent property-sector deleveraging and subdued domestic consumption. Hong Kong's Hang Seng tracked near **25,895** in mid-August trading (approx., verify before merging), pressured by elevated energy import costs, ongoing US-China trade tension as a secondary geopolitical variable, and sensitivity to global risk-off episodes triggered by the month-end Iran strikes.

Across APAC, two competing forces defined the investment landscape in August: the structural AI hardware demand cycle — which directly benefited Taiwanese semiconductor names and Korean memory producers — and the macro headwind of sharply higher energy import costs for the region's major oil-importing economies. Japan, South Korea, and China collectively import more than 10 million barrels per day, making the Brent crude surge from the Hormuz supply squeeze a meaningful drag on corporate and sovereign fiscal arithmetic.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US Dollar Index (DXY) was broadly range-bound through most of August, beginning the month near **99.78** and averaging approximately **100.12** across the period, before firming in the final week following Federal Reserve Chair Warsh's unexpectedly hawkish Jackson Hole speech. The post-Warsh repricing of rate expectations — September hike odds surging to **67%** — provided the most significant directional catalyst for the dollar of the month, partially offsetting earlier mild dollar weakness driven by the tame July CPI print.

EUR/USD traded near **1.1593** through mid-August, with the pair facing headwinds as the ECB's tightening cycle appeared to be approaching its terminal rate, reducing forward rate-differential support for the euro versus the increasingly hawkish Fed outlook. GBP/USD held near **1.3559**, broadly stable as the Bank of England maintained its data-dependent posture and UK growth data remained resilient. USD/JPY held elevated near **157**, as yen carry-trade selling overwhelmed the BOJ's hawkish signalling — the US-Japan rate differential remaining decisively in favour of yen-funded carry strategies.

The US-Iran strikes on August 30 generated a brief competing safe-haven bid for the yen and Swiss franc, though the overriding FX narrative of the month's final sessions was dollar firming on the Warsh-driven rate repricing. Structurally, the DXY remains significantly below its January 2025 peak above **109**, reflecting the secular erosion of US growth exceptionalism, though the dual tailwinds of geopolitical safe-haven demand and renewed rate-hike pricing have arrested the bear-dollar trend that entered 2026 with strong conviction.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
August 2026 was an exceptional month for commodities, headlined by a historic energy rally and continued gold outperformance. Brent crude advanced **+8.39%** to settle at **$90.80/bbl** on August 31, after touching an intra-month high near **$95/bbl** as Middle East Strait of Hormuz disruptions intensified throughout the month. WTI crude finished near **$87/bbl**, with the energy price complex up approximately **+8.8%** in aggregate as natural gas contributed **+10.1%** to the broader index, reflecting the cascading supply-chain effects of the ongoing Iran conflict on global LNG markets.

Gold was the month's standout performer, surging **+8.51%** from an August open near **$4,083/oz** to close at **$4,431/oz** — driven by the convergence of Middle East safe-haven demand, broadly range-bound dollar conditions, and sustained structural central-bank accumulation. An intraday peak of **$4,509** on August 13 illustrated the intensity of the safe-haven bid before partial profit-taking emerged; the month-end US-Iran strikes provided a further safe-haven spike that lifted the final settlement. Copper traded near **$6.35/lb** (approx., verify before merging) on COMEX, supported by structural demand from AI data-centre construction and global energy-transition infrastructure against a backdrop of constrained mine supply growth.

The energy supply shock carries cascading implications for the broader commodity complex: elevated crude and gas costs are feeding directly into fertiliser, petrochemical, and container shipping prices, creating a broad-based inflationary impulse that is structurally distinct from demand-driven commodity cycles and considerably more resistant to central-bank rate policy as a corrective tool.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
August was a difficult month for fixed income. US Treasury yields drifted higher in a bear-flattening pattern, with the 10-year yield ending at **4.73%** — up from **4.68%** at mid-month — and the 2-year yield closing at **4.34%**, up from **4.17%** in early August. The 10-year/2-year spread compressed from approximately **51bps** to **39bps** over the course of the month, as the front end repriced more aggressively following the Warsh Jackson Hole shock. The 30-year UST briefly topped **5.34%**, its highest level since the summer of 2007.

Federal Reserve Chair Warsh's August 28 keynote was the pivotal fixed income event of the month. By signalling that the Fed "may still have work to do" on inflation and declining to anchor any easing timeline, Warsh catalysed a violent short-end repricing: September rate-hike probability surged from **36%** to **67%** in a single session, compressing the curve and extending duration losses for investors positioned for the consensus easing cycle. The energy-driven inflation re-acceleration provided the fundamental justification for Warsh's hawkish stance, with crude's **+8.39%** monthly gain threatening to reverse the carefully accumulated progress on headline disinflation.

Credit markets proved more resilient than rates: investment-grade spreads held in well, and high-yield spreads widened only modestly, reflecting the constructive corporate earnings backdrop that simultaneously argued against rates optimism but supported credit quality. Globally, G10 sovereign yields rose in sympathy with Treasuries as the Warsh shock propagated through the rate complex, though core eurozone bonds received a partial offsetting bid from safe-haven flows generated by the US-Iran strikes at month-end.
